title: Pharmaceutical water system design, URS to DQ | Aquemi
meta: Water system design your quality unit can qualify: URS review, basis of design, P&IDs, functional specification and ICH Q9 risk assessment, ready for DQ.
eyebrow: PROCESS DESIGN · URS TO DESIGN QUALIFICATION · EU GMP ANNEX 15 · ASTM E2500 · ICH Q9
headline: Water system design traced to your URS, approved at DQ and built to qualify
lead: EU GMP Annex 15 makes the user requirement specification (URS) the point of reference for the whole validation lifecycle, and asks that design qualification (DQ) verify every one of its requirements. We turn your URS into a basis of design, mass balance, piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs) and a functional specification in which each requirement carries an ID, traced to the drawing that meets it and the test that proves it at factory acceptance testing (FAT), site acceptance testing (SAT) and installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ). A risk assessment to ICH Q9(R1) marks the critical design elements, so qualification effort goes where water quality is decided.

blocks.h: Most qualification problems are designed in, long before the IQ protocol is written
body: A loop sized on an average draw fails turbulent flow at peak. A branch drawn without its length fails the dead leg check at IQ. A divert setpoint that lives only in the programmer's head becomes an OQ deviation. Each of these is cheap to fix on a drawing and expensive to fix in a qualified room.

So we write the design to be checked. Every URS line gets an ID and a written answer: met, met with a condition, or not met and why. The basis of design records each sizing decision with the data behind it. The functional specification states every setpoint, alarm and interlock as a testable sentence. The P&IDs carry the instrument tags and dead leg dimensions the IQ protocol will verify.

That is what Annex 15 (3.2 and 3.3) asks of a URS and a DQ, and what ASTM E2500 and the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5 for commissioning and qualification (C&Q) build on: specify from product and process requirements, find the critical aspects by risk assessment, and verify them once, at the point where the evidence is best.

blocks.h: How a requirement travels from your URS to qualification
blocks.caption: Each URS line carries its ID through every document. The basis of design says how it is met, the functional specification (FS) and P&IDs show where, the risk assessment says how critical it is, design review confirms it before steel is cut, and the commissioning and qualification plan names the test that proves it. Nothing reaches IQ or OQ without a requirement behind it, and no requirement is left without a test.

blocks.h: Questions engineering, validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Our URS is a draft. Is it too early to send it?
items.a: No. A draft is the best time. Annex 15, 3.2 says the essential elements of quality should be built in at the URS stage, and the cheapest change is a sentence. We return the compliance matrix with gaps, conflicting requirements and requirements no one could test, each with a proposed wording. The URS stays yours to approve.

items.q: Who owns DQ: you or us?
items.a: You do. Annex 15, 3.3 describes DQ as the documented verification that the design meets GMP and the URS, and the 2025 revision of ASTM E2500 calls for quality unit approval of it. We supply the design review report, the traceability matrix and the risk assessment as evidence, in your template if you have one. Your quality unit decides.

items.q: Can tests at FAT count towards qualification?
items.a: Where it is justified. Annex 15, 3.6 allows documentation review and some tests at FAT without repeating them at IQ/OQ, if you can show transport and installation do not affect the function. We plan which tests qualify for that in the commissioning and qualification plan during detailed design, and write the FAT protocol so your quality unit can review and approve it before execution.

items.q: Our site does not use ASTM E2500. Does that change your design?
items.a: Not the documents. The basis of design, P&IDs, functional specification and risk assessment are the same. What changes is how much is verified, by whom and how often it is repeated. We deliver in the qualification approach your procedures describe.

items.q: Which risk assessment method do you use?
items.a: ICH Q9(R1) does not prescribe one. For water systems we usually run a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) at component and function level, with your quality and engineering leads in the room, because the people who will operate the system know failure modes a designer misses. We use your template and scoring if your procedures set one. The output is a list of critical aspects and critical design elements, and the verification each needs.

items.q: Can you work with our engineering firm's design?
items.a: Yes. We can design the water system inside a package your architect-engineer leads, with our P&IDs, GA drawings and utility list issued for their drawings, or review a water system design they have produced against your URS and the standards above. [State whether a design-only or design review engagement is sold separately from equipment, and how it is priced.]

items.q: Are the drawings sealed by a professional engineer?
items.a: [State whether drawings and pressure vessel calculations are sealed by a licensed professional engineer (P.Eng.), and in which provinces.]

items.q: What happens if our requirements change after design freeze?
items.a: The change goes through change control. We state which documents it touches, whether it affects a critical aspect or critical design element, and what has to be re-reviewed or retested, before you decide. Changes that touch no critical element can usually follow the engineering change process, as ASTM E2500 allows.

items.q: Do you design for future capacity?
items.a: Yes, for the expansion you name. We size the loop and tank for it or add capped tie-in points, and state in the basis of design what a later phase would need, so a second phase does not mean a new loop or a new qualification of the whole system.

items.q: Do we own the drawings and the native files?
items.a: [State what the customer receives: drawing formats (PDF and native CAD), ownership or licence terms, and the design software used.]

items.q: Is design charged separately, or credited against the equipment?
items.a: [State whether the URS review is free, and whether concept or design fees are credited against an equipment order.]

items.q: How can our quality unit audit your quality system before awarding a design contract?
items.a: [Confirm: the quality management system Aquemi runs and the standard it follows.] We welcome a supplier audit before you award the contract, on site at [engineering office location] or remote, and share our quality manual [openly or under NDA].

items.q: What happens if a gap shows up at DQ or at IQ/OQ?
items.a: If it traces to a requirement we accepted in the basis of design, we correct the design, revise the drawings and update the affected qualification documents [at our cost, or under the stated design warranty terms]. If it is a new requirement, it goes through change control with its cost and schedule effect stated before any work starts.
